editorNote: Apple gives the Macintosh room to breathe while AtariSoft brings arcade stars to competing home computers.
morningLine: This week in 1984: the Macintosh gets 512K, and the game shelf ignores hardware boundaries.

lead.headline: Apple Unveils a 512K Macintosh
lead.dek: Four times the memory gives the little graphical computer room to breathe.
body: Apple opened the week on September 10 with the Macintosh 512K, its first major revision of the compact machine introduced in January. The familiar all-in-one case still houses a nine-inch black-and-white display and a Motorola 68000 processor, but the built-in memory leaps from 128K to 512K. That fourfold increase tackles the original Macintosh’s most conspicuous limitation.

The extra RAM gives bigger documents and applications more working room and makes the computer a more practical proposition for people who spend a full day inside its graphical desktop. Early owners had learned how quickly 128K could disappear when a program, document and system software all needed space at once. The new machine does not change the single 400K floppy drive, but it gives software a much larger workbench.

The Centre for Computing History lists the new machine at $3,195. That puts the improved Macintosh well above the bargain PC compatibles crowding shop windows this autumn. Apple is asking buyers to value the integrated screen, mouse-driven interface and growing application library over cheaper configurations with a familiar IBM-style command line.

The “Fat Mac,” as the memory-rich revision is becoming known, is therefore less a new look than a bet on what the Macintosh can do when software has room to grow. For owners who liked the original machine but found its memory cramped, this week’s announcement is a consequential upgrade; for undecided shoppers, it sharpens the choice between graphical ease and price.

stories.headline: AtariSoft Sends Arcade Favorites Across the Home-Computer Aisle
body: AtariSoft’s September advertisement puts six new titles in front of owners of rival computers: Gremlins, Crystal Castles, Donkey Kong Jr., Mario Bros., Track & Field and Typo Attack. The line spans combinations of Commodore 64, Apple II, IBM PC, PCjr and VIC-20 versions, making familiar arcade names a selling point well beyond Atari’s own hardware.

The catalog also keeps Pac-Man, Ms. Pac-Man, Jungle Hunt, Battlezone, Donkey Kong, Centipede and Pole Position in circulation. Its small print stresses that these editions are not made or approved by the rival computer manufacturers. The more important message at the game counter is that a good title can travel with players from one machine to another.

stories.headline: PC Compatibles Compete on Price, Portability and Speed
body: The IBM-compatible aisle is filling fast. In September’s Creative Computing, Otrona offers a 19-pound 2001 portable with a seven-inch amber display, 8088 processor, 360K floppy and 128K of RAM for $2,495. Heathkit’s heavier HS-161 brings a nine-inch screen and pop-up floppy drives; a two-drive assembled model lists for $3,199.

At the desktop end, Tava lists a two-drive PC at $1,995 and a faster Turbo Tava at $2,495. These machines compete on price or portability, yet compatibility is not a single promise: shoppers must ask whether a favorite program depends on IBM hardware behavior or merely reads a DOS disk. The expanding choice is good news for buyers willing to examine the details.

stories.headline: Framework Packs Six Office Tools Into One Box
body: Ashton-Tate’s Framework brings word processing, spreadsheet, business graphics, data management, forms processing and outlining to an IBM PC package priced at $695. The program requires 256K of RAM, a reminder that integrated software is demanding more from the office machine even as it promises fewer trips between separate disks.

Computer Creations offers a lower-priced answer with The Ultimate at $249.50, combining writing, database, mail merge and a link to the Postal Service’s E-COM system. The two products make the same argument from different price points: an office computer should let workers move among jobs without rebuilding their day around separate applications.

worldAnchor.headline: Hurricane Diana menaces the Carolina coast
worldAnchor.summary: On September 10-11, Hurricane Diana strengthened and threatened the Carolinas; contemporary UPI dispatches described 110 mph winds and the storm bearing down on Cape Fear and the Grand Strand.

gadgetWatch.headline: Revox's $1,150 CD player remembers its program when unplugged
gadgetWatch.summary: Audio's September test praised the Studer-Revox B225, a four-times-oversampling Compact Disc player with 19-step programming, track- or time-based selection, looping, automatic pauses, a calibration tone and nonvolatile memory. The optional infrared remote cost $125.

bbsNote.headline: Creative Computing opens a two-way clubhouse on CompuServe
bbsNote.summary: The magazine's September telecommunications column described its new CompuServe Special Interest Group, launched in May, as a lively direct line between staff and readers. Public message boards, downloadable data sections, online conferences and a frequently updated street-price index show the increasingly social and practical character of dial-up computing.

posts.text: Users could leave and reply to public messages; the column warned there was no private messaging in the SIG and recommended E-Mail for private exchanges.
A CB-style conference area offered as many as 30 channels and was mainly used for scheduled live conferences.
The SIG promised maintained street prices for popular computers, ten printers, seven monitors and twenty software packages.

posts.platform: Washington Apple Pi / CompuServe / Apple BBS
posts.text: The September Washington Apple Pi Journal carried both 'Calling CompuServe with Apple III' and sysop Tom Warrick's 'Your Own Apple Bulletin Board,' documenting a user group moving between national service and local BBS culture.

curiosity.headline: A PC-compatible kit that weighed 35 pounds
curiosity.summary: Heathkit called the HS-161 portable, but carrying it meant hauling 35 pounds of computer.
curiosity.detail: The luggable's two floppy drives popped up from the case; it included a 9-inch amber screen and detachable keyboard. The assembled two-drive version cost $3,199, while Creative Computing estimated the still-unannounced kit price would be $700-$800 less.
